description: Nova Ltd. engages in the design, development, production, and sale of process control systems used in the manufacture of semiconductors in Taiwan, the United States, China, Korea, and internationally.
description_full: Nova Ltd. engages in the design, development, production, and sale of process control systems used in the manufacture of semiconductors in Taiwan, the United States, China, Korea, and internationally. The company's product portfolio includes a set of metrology platforms for dimensional, films, and materials and chemical metrology measurements for process control for various semiconductor manufacturing process steps, such as lithography, Etch, chemical mechanical planarization, deposition, electrochemical plating, and advanced packaging. It serves various sectors of the integrated circuit manufacturing industry, including logic, foundry, memory, and packaging sectors, as well as process equipment manufacturers. Nova Ltd. was formerly known as Nova Measuring Instruments Ltd. and changed its name to Nova Ltd. in July 2021. Nova Ltd. was incorporated in 1993 and is headquartered in Rehovot, Israel.

financial_summary: Nova Ltd. is a large-cap technology business with a $10.1B market cap on $881M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years and +19% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 33% against a 11% cost of capital — a 21-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 56% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $218M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.95× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 0.3%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 29% operating margin runs 22pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.23x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+16.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 15% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 20% over the last three months.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 48% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 60% and a beta of 1.38, it amplifies market moves.
Liquidity is deep, with about $121.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 53% in the 2022 bear market and 85% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $271 (margin of safety -17%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 14%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $138 to $547 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: P/E 36.4 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 31.2 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 46.4 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 24% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $406 on average, 28% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 33% clears the cost of capital of 11.3% by 21pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.60).
It runs a 56% gross margin and converts 25% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 20% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 16.3% of revenue on R&D and 3.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $536.3M (5% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.8, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 196 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
The Beneish M-score (-1.90) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 15.6% over 3 years, 26.7% over 5 years and 19.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 32.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs 2.1x depreciation (3.1% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 48, clearing the bar for a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 67%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (10 sales, net $6.1M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.3% (0.3% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 2.4% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 1,612 employees, each generates about $546K of revenue, 1.5x the Technology median, and revenue has grown 16.6% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $135K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $437K (1x revenue per employee).
